title: Homophones and homographs
subtitle: weather / whether, a row / a row
summary: Learn to tell apart words that sound alike but are spelt differently (homophones) and words spelt alike but with different meanings (homographs).

lesson.heading: Two kinds of confusing pair
lesson.text: **Homophones** are words with different meanings which sound the same but are spelt differently, so only the spelling tells you which one is meant. **Homographs** are words which are written in the same way but have different meanings, and they may even be said differently.

examples.text: **row** as in 'at the end of the row' and **roe** as in 'fish eggs' - homophones.
We had a **row** about who should pay for the tickets.
He sat at the end of the **row**.
examples.note: row here = a line of seats - the same spelling, a different word

lesson.heading: Common homophones (1)
rows: the air we breathe / the person who will inherit
smash or damage / stop a vehicle
the price of a ticket / just, or light-coloured, or a funfair
the metal frame you burn coal in / wonderful
a deep sound of pain / past participle of grow
with a rough voice / the animal
belonging to it / it is, it has

lesson.heading: Common homophones (2)
rows: a sheet of glass / what you feel when you are hurt
the ringing of bells / the skin of a fruit
speak to God / an animal that is hunted
the cloth on a boat / selling something
something you see / a place where something is built or dug
the bottom of a shoe or foot / the spirit
the middle of your body / use badly, or rubbish
rain, sun, wind / if, in indirect questions
complain in a high voice / the drink

lesson.heading: Homographs: one spelling, two meanings
rows: I **live** in the north of England. (reside)
My favourite group is singing **live** on TV. (not recorded)
I **read** War and Peace last year. (past)
The **lead** singer in the group is great. (main)
The **wind** blew the tree down. (moving air)
She **wound** the string round the parcel. (past of wind)
He suffered a terrible **wound** in the war. (injury)
This book is called English Vocabulary in **Use**. (noun)
You must know how to **use** words. (verb)
They lived in a large old **house**. (noun)
The **sow** has five piglets. (a female pig)
The farmers **sow** the seeds in spring. (plant)
The violinist wore a **bow** tie. (a knot)
He made a **bow** to the audience. (bend forward)

lesson.heading: The classic mistake: weather or whether?

left.label: whether = if
left.text: Use **whether** when you are talking about a choice between possibilities.
examples: I don't know **whether** to go or not.

right.label: weather = rain, sun, wind
right.text: Use **weather** only for the conditions outside.
examples: **Whether** we have a picnic tomorrow will depend on the **weather**.

lesson.note: Say: I don't know whether to go or not. Not: I don't know ~~weather~~ to go or not.

lesson.text: Homophones and homographs are behind most English jokes and puns - if a joke makes no sense, look for a word that has a second meaning.

exercises.prompt: Match each spelling with its meaning.

pairs.right: the middle part of your body

exercises.prompt: I really must do some more exercise or I'll never lose ___.
exercises.explanation: Weight is what the scales show; wait means stay until something happens.

exercises.prompt: Watching TV game shows is such a ___ of time.
exercises.explanation: Waste = a bad use of something. Your waist is the middle of your body.

exercises.prompt: There's a hole in the ___ of my shoe.
exercises.explanation: The sole is the bottom of a shoe; the soul is the spirit.

exercises.prompt: You are not ___ to talk during the test.
exercises.explanation: Allowed = permitted. Aloud means out loud, not silently.

exercises.prompt: Don't throw away that orange ___. I need it for a recipe.
exercises.explanation: Peel is the skin of a fruit; a peal is the ringing of bells.

exercises.prompt: He's going ___ a rather difficult ___ at the moment.
exercises.explanation: Through = from one side to the other; a phase is a period of time. Threw is the past of throw and faze means disturb.

exercises.prompt: In 'The buildings **house** a library and two concert halls', what does *house* mean?
exercises.explanation: House is a homograph: the noun is a building, the verb means contain or provide space for.

exercises.prompt: In 'He's the **lead** singer in the group', what does *lead* mean?
exercises.explanation: Lead is a homograph: the main singer, or the metal used in old pipes.

exercises.statement: In 'I **wound** the rope around the tree', *wound* is the past tense of *wind*.
exercises.explanation: Correct - the other wound, meaning an injury, is a completely different word with the same spelling.

exercises.statement: In 'The **sow** has five piglets', *sow* means to plant seeds.
exercises.explanation: Here a sow is a female pig. Farmers sow seeds - the same spelling, a different word.

exercises.prompt: Match the two halves of these children's jokes. Each one plays on a word with two meanings.

pairs.left: What do you get if you cross a sheep and a kangaroo?
What did the south wind say to the north wind?
Why did the man take his pencil to bed?
pairs.right: He wanted to draw the curtains.

pairs.left: Why is history the sweetest lesson?

pairs.right: A drum takes a lot of beating.

exercises.prompt: Put the sentence in order. It contains two homophones.
exercises.answer: Brake now or you'll break that toy in the road.
exercises.explanation: Brake is what you do to stop a car; break means damage or smash.
